subject: Biology
title: Cell Structure and Biophysics
outline: State the cell theory and the contributions of Hooke, Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow
Draw and label generalised plant and animal cells
Relate the structure of each organelle to its function
Compare plant and animal cells and prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
Explain diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, turgidity and active transport
Calculate and interpret surface area to volume ratios

modules.title: Cell Theory and Cell Structure
modules.html:
1. Historical Development

  • Robert Hooke (1665) examined cork with a simple microscope and coined the word 'cell'.
  • Leeuwenhoek (1674) observed living micro-organisms (animalcules).
  • Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839) proposed that all plants and animals are made of cells.
  • Virchow (1855) added omnis cellula e cellula – every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.

2. The Cell Theory

  1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
  2. The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
  3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.
  4. Cells contain hereditary material passed to daughter cells.

3. Organelles and Their Functions

StructureFunction
Cell (plasma) membraneSelectively permeable boundary controlling entry and exit of substances; fluid-mosaic of phospholipid bilayer with proteins
Cell wall (plants)Rigid cellulose layer giving shape, support and protection; fully permeable
NucleusContains chromatin (DNA); controls all cell activities and heredity
MitochondrionSite of aerobic respiration; 'powerhouse' producing ATP; has cristae
ChloroplastContains chlorophyll on grana; site of photosynthesis
RibosomeSite of protein synthesis
Endoplasmic reticulumRough ER transports proteins; smooth ER makes lipids
Golgi bodyPackages, modifies and secretes materials
LysosomeContains hydrolytic enzymes for digestion of worn-out structures
VacuoleLarge and central in plants; stores cell sap and maintains turgor
CentrioleOrganises spindle fibres during animal cell division

4. Comparisons

Plant cellAnimal cell
Cellulose cell wall presentAbsent
Chloroplasts usually presentAbsent
Large central vacuoleSmall, temporary vacuoles
Fixed, regular shapeIrregular, flexible shape
Stores starchStores glycogen
Centrioles usually absentCentrioles present

Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have no nuclear membrane, no mitochondria, no ER and possess 70S ribosomes and a peptidoglycan wall; eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

examples.q: Why do muscle and sperm cells contain very many mitochondria?
examples.a: Both require large, continuous supplies of ATP — muscle cells for contraction and sperm cells for flagellar swimming. Since mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration and ATP production, their number reflects the energy demand of the cell.

examples.q: A cell is placed in distilled water and does not burst. Suggest the type of cell.
examples.a: It is a plant cell. Its rigid cellulose cell wall exerts an inward wall pressure that balances the increasing turgor pressure, so the cell becomes turgid instead of bursting. An animal cell without a wall would undergo haemolysis/cytolysis.

modules.title: Biophysics: Diffusion, Osmosis and Active Transport
modules.html:
1. Diffusion

Diffusion is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration along a concentration gradient, until equilibrium is reached. It is passive (no ATP required). Rate of diffusion increases with temperature, concentration gradient and surface area, and decreases with molecular size and diffusion distance (Fick’s principle):

$$\text{Rate of diffusion} \propto \frac{\text{surface area} \times \text{concentration difference}}{\text{thickness of membrane}}$$

Biological examples: gaseous exchange in alveoli and leaves, absorption of digested food, spread of perfume.

2. Osmosis

Osmosis is the movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential (dilute/hypotonic solution) to a region of lower water potential (concentrated/hypertonic solution) through a semi-permeable membrane. Water potential relationships are summarised as:

$$\Psi_{cell} = \Psi_{s} + \Psi_{p}$$

where \( \Psi_{s} \) is the solute (osmotic) potential and \( \Psi_{p} \) the pressure (turgor) potential.

  • Turgidity – a plant cell in a hypotonic solution gains water, the vacuole swells and the cell becomes firm; turgor supports herbaceous stems and opens stomata.
  • Plasmolysis – in a hypertonic solution water leaves the cell, the protoplasm shrinks away from the wall. The point at which plasmolysis just begins is incipient plasmolysis. Reversal by placing in water is deplasmolysis.
  • Haemolysis – bursting of a red blood cell in a hypotonic solution; crenation is its shrinking in a hypertonic solution.

3. Active Transport

Active transport is the movement of substances against a concentration gradient, using energy from ATP and specific carrier proteins in the membrane. Evidence includes reduced uptake when respiration is inhibited by cyanide or low oxygen. Examples: absorption of mineral salts by root hairs, reabsorption of glucose in the kidney tubule, the sodium–potassium pump in nerve cells.

FeatureDiffusion/OsmosisActive transport
GradientDown the gradientAgainst the gradient
EnergyNoneATP required
CarriersNot alwaysAlways specific carriers
Effect of cyanideUnaffectedStopped

examples.q: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 1 cm and of side 2 cm, and state the biological significance.
examples.a: For side 1 cm: \( SA = 6 \times 1^2 = 6\,\text{cm}^2 \), \( V = 1^3 = 1\,\text{cm}^3 \), ratio \( = 6:1 \). For side 2 cm: \( SA = 6 \times 2^2 = 24\,\text{cm}^2 \), \( V = 8\,\text{cm}^3 \), ratio \( = 3:1 \). Small organisms therefore have a larger surface area per unit volume and can rely on simple diffusion, while large organisms need specialised transport and respiratory surfaces.

examples.q: Fresh potato cylinders placed in strong salt solution became flabby. Explain.
examples.a: The salt solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so water moved out of the potato cells by osmosis. The cells lost turgor and became flaccid (plasmolysed), so the tissue as a whole became soft and reduced in length and mass.

modules.title: Cell Specialisation and Practical Microscopy
modules.html:
1. Specialised Cells and Their Adaptations

CellAdaptationFunction
Root hair cellLong extension, thin wall, many mitochondriaAbsorbs water and mineral salts
Palisade mesophyllColumn-shaped, many chloroplastsTraps maximum light for photosynthesis
Red blood cellBiconcave, no nucleus, haemoglobinTransports oxygen
Nerve cellLong axon, myelin sheathRapid impulse transmission
Sperm cellFlagellum, acrosome, mitochondriaSwims to and penetrates the ovum
Xylem vesselDead, lignified, hollow tubeConducts water and gives support

2. Using the Light Microscope

  • Total magnification = magnification of eyepiece × magnification of objective. With a ×10 eyepiece and ×40 objective, \( M = 10 \times 40 = 400 \).
  • Actual size is obtained from \( \text{actual size} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{magnification}} \).
  • Thin sections, staining (iodine for starch, methylene blue for nuclei) and correct illumination give clear images.

3. Protoplasm

Protoplasm is the living content of a cell: cytoplasm plus nucleus. It is about 70–90 % water and contains proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, nucleic acids and mineral salts. It is colloidal, capable of movement (cyclosis), irritable and metabolically active.

examples.q: A cell measures 50 mm on a drawing whose magnification is ×500. Find its actual size in micrometres.
State two ways the root hair cell is adapted for absorption.
examples.a: (i) The hair-like projection greatly increases the surface area for water and ion uptake. (ii) It has a thin, permeable wall and numerous mitochondria supplying ATP for the active transport of mineral ions.

quiz.q: The scientist who first used the term 'cell' was
quiz.solution: Hooke saw empty box-like compartments in cork in 1665 and named them cells.

quiz.q: Which statement completes the cell theory?
options: All cells come from pre-existing cells
quiz.solution: Virchow's principle omnis cellula e cellula completed the theory.

quiz.q: The organelle described as the powerhouse of the cell is the
quiz.solution: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and release ATP.

quiz.q: Protein synthesis takes place on the
A structure present in plant cells but absent in animal cells is the
quiz.solution: Only plant cells have a rigid cellulose wall outside the plasma membrane.

quiz.q: Digestive enzymes within a cell are contained in the
quiz.solution: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material.

quiz.q: The cell membrane is best described as
quiz.solution: It allows some substances through while restricting others, hence selectively (differentially) permeable.

options: solute from high to low concentration
water from higher to lower water potential through a semi-permeable membrane
ions against a gradient using ATP
quiz.solution: Osmosis concerns water movement across a semi-permeable membrane down a water-potential gradient.

quiz.q: A plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution will
quiz.solution: Water leaves the cell, the protoplast shrinks from the wall and the cell becomes plasmolysed.

quiz.q: A red blood cell placed in distilled water will
quiz.solution: Water enters by osmosis and, lacking a cell wall, the cell swells and bursts (haemolysis).

quiz.q: Which process requires energy from ATP?
quiz.solution: Only active transport moves substances against the concentration gradient, using ATP and carrier proteins.

quiz.q: The surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 3 cm is
Cyanide stops the uptake of mineral ions by root hairs because it
quiz.solution: Active transport depends on ATP from respiration, which cyanide blocks.

quiz.q: Total magnification with a ×5 eyepiece and ×40 objective is
The chloroplast pigment that traps light energy is
quiz.solution: Chlorophyll on the grana absorbs mainly red and blue light for photosynthesis.

quiz.q: Turgor pressure in plant cells is important because it
options: supports herbaceous stems and opens stomata
quiz.solution: Turgid cells press against one another, keeping soft tissues firm and driving stomatal opening.
